Hook: On Friday the seventeenth of April 2020, a barrel of American crude oil for delivery in May sold for 17.73 dollars. The world had stopped driving and flying, and the oil nobody was burning had to go somewhere. Much of America's went into the tanks at Cushing, Oklahoma, where that contract is delivered. By the seventeenth, the tanks there were 76 percent full, and some of the empty space was already leased to others. On Monday, anyone still holding the contract would have to take the oil, with nowhere to put it. So they paid others to take it. The contract settled at minus 37.63 dollars a barrel. For a day, a barrel of oil was worth less than nothing: whoever took it was paid almost thirty-eight dollars.

Six years later, the opposite. About a fifth of the world's oil sails out of the Persian Gulf through one narrow strait, between Iran and Oman: some twenty million barrels a day. On the twenty-eighth of February 2026, war came to the region, and most ships stopped passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude had begun the year at 61 dollars a barrel. By the end of March it was 118. In October it averaged 124. The same black liquid. Minus thirty-seven dollars one spring, a hundred and twenty-four another. This part is about why: what a barrel costs to get out of the ground, who owns it, and who, or what, decides what it sells for.
Industry, Built. Part eight: oil and gas. What does a barrel cost, and who decides what it sells for?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: drill, wait, or buy back.

Play it yourself. You run an oil company, oil sells for ninety dollars a barrel, and you have three projects on the table. A conventional field on land: 700 million dollars, first oil in two years, and its wells fade slowly, by about a tenth in their first year. It pays its way at about 34 dollars a barrel. A deepwater platform: six billion dollars, five years before the first barrel, and half a billion barrels after that. It needs about 49. A pad of ten shale wells: a hundred and twenty million dollars, oil within the year, but each well's output falls by 60 percent in its first year. It needs about 61. Or you can drill nothing, and hand the money back to your shareholders. Pause, and choose. Remember that you are betting on the price of oil for as long as the project lasts.

Now let the price wander, as it does. Here are forty of four hundred futures for the price, each starting at ninety and drifting, with shocks every year, towards seventy. Run each project through all four hundred. The conventional field almost never loses: on average, each dollar spent on it adds about 2.2 dollars of value, in today's money. The deepwater platform makes the most money in total, but you wait five years for it, and in 8 percent of the futures it loses. The shale pad loses in 12 percent, but you know within two years whether you were right, and you can stop. So the cheap, slow field is the prize, if you can get one, and the rest of this part shows who has them. The giant project is a bet on the price a decade away. The short project is the one you can stop. Every oil company is a mix of these three bets, and the price it assumes matters more than anything else it decides.
Decline: Chapter three. A well, and how it fades.

On the tenth of January 1901, near Beaumont, Texas, a well at a hill called Spindletop blew six tons of drilling pipe out of the ground, and then oil, a hundred feet into the air. It flowed, by one estimate, a hundred thousand barrels a day until it was capped nine days later. Hundreds of wells followed it onto the hill. In 1902 the field produced seventeen and a half million barrels, about forty-eight thousand a day. By February 1904 it was down to ten thousand. Some of the biggest names in oil were born or grew up there: the Texas Company, later Texaco, Gulf Oil, and Humble, which became part of Exxon. And the first lesson of the oil business was learned there too: every well fades.

Oil flows because the rock is under pressure, and every barrel that comes out lets a little of the pressure go. So a well's output falls, fast at first and then more slowly. In 1945 an engineer, J. J. Arps, wrote down the curve that petroleum engineers still use. A conventional well into a big, porous reservoir fades gently: in our model, by about a tenth in its first year. A shale well is different. The rock is so tight that the oil comes mostly from the cracks that were made, close to the well, and once that is drained the flow drops. Our model shale well loses 60 percent of its output in its first year, and keeps falling.

Put thousands of such wells together and you have a treadmill. To hold a shale basin at a million barrels a day, our model needs about 44 new wells every month, for ever, each one replacing the fading output of the ones before. Stop drilling, and output falls by about 21 percent within a year, and keeps falling. That is the shale business: less like mining a deposit, more like running a factory whose product evaporates. It is also why shale can respond to prices within months, in both directions, as Chapter 11 shows.
Reserves: Chapter four. Reserves are an economic number.

How much oil does a company have? There are three answers, nested inside each other. All the oil in the rock, wherever it is: most of it will never come out. The part that could come out with today's methods. In 1956 the geologist King Hubbert reckoned only about a third of the oil underground was being recovered; better methods keep raising that share. And the part worth producing at today's prices and costs: proved reserves, the number a company reports. For companies listed in America, the Securities and Exchange Commission sets the price to use: the average of the last twelve months. So a company's reserves can shrink, or grow, without a single barrel moving.

Here is what that means for the biggest American oil company. At the end of 2019 ExxonMobil reported 22.4 billion barrels of oil and gas, as oil equivalent, in proved reserves. Each square is a hundred million barrels. Then 2020: oil prices collapsed, and the twelve-month average fell with them. At that price, 3.1 billion barrels of tar at Kearl, in Canada's oil sands, no longer paid, and so no longer counted. More went in Canada and the United States, and cuts to drilling plans took more. Proved reserves fell to 15.2 billion barrels. Nothing had been pumped, and nothing had leaked. The oil was exactly where it had been. A year later, prices recovered and reserves were back to 18.5; at the end of 2025, 19.3. Reserves are not a quantity of rock. They are a forecast, at a price.
Cost: Chapter five. What a barrel costs.

What does a barrel of oil cost? It depends whose, and what you count. Saudi Aramco, the state oil company of Saudi Arabia, reports what it costs to lift a barrel out of its fields: 3.51 dollars in 2025. Add what it spends on new wells and plant, another 8 dollars a barrel, and it is still under twelve. Every year the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas asks American oil executives two questions. What price do you need to keep your existing wells running? This spring, on average, 43 dollars. And what price do you need to drill a new well and make money on it? 66 dollars; in the Permian Basin of Texas and New Mexico, 67. Brent averaged sixty-nine dollars in 2025. At that price, Saudi Arabia's barrels earned fortunes, and an American driller was close to the line on a new well.

Part 4 showed why both numbers matter. Line up the world's barrels from cheapest to dearest: the giant fields of the Gulf states first, then other conventional fields, deep water, oil sands, and last, the new American shale wells. When the world wants this much oil, the last barrel it needs is a shale barrel. So over the long run, the price has to cover that barrel's cost, or it will not be drilled. Everyone cheaper keeps the difference. That difference, between a three-dollar barrel and a sixty-dollar price, is one of the largest sources of money in the world, and the next chapter asks who gets it.
Owners: Chapter six. Who owns the oil.

Start with who produces it. In 2025 the world produced about eighty-four and a half million barrels of crude oil a day. The largest producer was the United States, then Russia, then Saudi Arabia, Canada and Iraq. The countries in red belong to OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, which together produced 35 percent of it. But the bigger difference is who owns the oil. In America, much of it belongs to whoever owns the land, and is produced by thousands of private companies. In most other places, the oil under the ground belongs to the state.

Compare two companies. Saudi Aramco holds, under its concession from the Saudi state, about 247 billion barrels of oil and gas, counted as oil equivalent. ExxonMobil, the largest American oil company, reported 19.3 billion of proved reserves at the end of 2025. The two numbers are not measured under the same rules, but the difference in scale is not in doubt: the biggest oil companies in the world are mostly owned by states.

And when a barrel costs a few dollars to lift and sells for seventy, most of the difference goes to the owner of the rock. In 2025 Aramco paid the Saudi state 40 billion dollars in royalties and other taxes, and 94 billion in income tax and zakat. It then paid 86 billion dollars in dividends, and the Government, which owns 81 percent of the company directly, received about 70 billion of them. Much of the rest went to the state's own investment fund. All told, something like 204 billion dollars went from one company's barrels to one government in one year. That is why oil is as much about states as about companies, and why the chapters on OPEC and on war are in a film about an industry.
Pump: Chapter seven. Where a gallon's dollar goes.

Follow the money back from the pump. In August 2026, a gallon of regular gasoline in America cost 4.06 dollars on average. About half of it, 204 cents, paid for the crude oil it was made from. 99 cents went to refining it: the refiners' costs and their margin, unusually wide that summer. 51 cents paid for pipelines, trucks and the filling station. And 52 cents were taxes, federal and state, which are charged in cents a gallon, not as a share of the price.

Watch the shares move over twenty-six years. The crude-oil layer swells and shrinks with the price of a barrel: the peak of 2008, the collapse of 2009, the long slump after 2014, the spike after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The tax layer barely moves, because it is so many cents a gallon. So when prices were low, in 2000, taxes were 32 percent of the price; in 2026, 13 percent. And the refining layer, thin in most years, fattens whenever refineries are short of capacity, as Chapter 12 shows. The price at the pump is mostly a price of crude oil, set far away.
Price: Chapter eight. One price, many barrels.

There is no single price of oil. There are prices of particular crudes, at particular places, and a few of them are used as yardsticks for all the rest. West Texas Intermediate, a light American crude, delivered at Cushing. Brent, a blend of North Sea crudes loaded onto ships, the yardstick for most of the world's oil. And Dubai and Oman, for the heavier crudes of the Gulf, sold mostly to Asia. Every other crude is priced as a premium or a discount to one of these. Usually they move together. But in March 2026, with tankers unable to leave the Gulf, Brent rose much faster than American crude, which was not stuck behind the strait. By the end of the month Brent was 25 dollars a barrel above WTI.

Most oil is traded for delivery later, in futures contracts, and the price for each month ahead forms a curve. Usually oil for delivery in a year costs about the same as oil now, or a little less. But when there is far too much oil today, today's oil gets cheap and tomorrow's stays dear, and anyone with a tank can buy now, store it, and sell it forward at a profit. Traders call that contango. It lasts until the tanks are full. Which is what happened in April 2020. Almost every futures contract is closed out before it expires; only about one percent ends in a real delivery. But the tanks at Cushing were filling, refineries were running a quarter below normal, and on the last day of trading the people still holding May contracts could not take delivery. They paid others to take them off their hands. Brent, priced on oil at sea, never went below zero: on the next day it closed at nineteen dollars.
Swing: Chapter nine. Why the price swings so hard.

In the short run, almost nobody can change how much oil they use, or how much they produce. Drivers still drive to work, and planes still fly. That is a steep demand curve. And wells already pump flat out, while new ones take months or years. That is a steep supply curve. Now take away five percent of the supply. With both sides this unresponsive, the price has to rise by two-thirds before enough buyers give up enough oil. Make both sides twice as responsive, and the same shortage raises the price by less than a third. Small shortages, huge price moves: that is the arithmetic of a market where neither side can move quickly, and it is why oil's price swings more than almost anything else people buy every day.

2026 put the arithmetic to the test. At the worst, in May, almost eleven million barrels a day of Middle Eastern production was shut in, a tenth of the world's supply. The model says that should have nearly tripled the price. It did not, because the world found cushions: stocks were drawn down, Saudi Arabia pumped oil across the desert to the Red Sea, ships passed cargoes from one to another off Oman, and over the year production fell by less than five percent. Consumption fell by about two million barrels a day, mostly in China and the Middle East. Set the fall in use against the rise in price, and you get about 0.05: for every one percent rise in price, about 5 hundredths of a percent less oil used. It is a rough calculation, since other things changed too, but it is close to the steep demand curve we just drew.
Opec: Chapter ten. OPEC: a cartel's arithmetic.

A market where small shortages cause huge price swings invites a cartel: if a few producers hold oil back, together, the price rises by much more than the barrels they give up. OPEC was founded in 1960. By 1973 its members produced well over half the world's crude, and that autumn its Arab members cut supply and embargoed the United States; the price of a barrel more than doubled within months. But high prices did what high prices do. Oil from the North Sea, Alaska and Mexico came on, buyers learned to use less, and by 1985 OPEC's share was down to barely more than a quarter. It has been around a third ever since.

The cartel's arithmetic has a catch, and Saudi Arabia found it. To hold the price up as demand fell and new oil arrived, someone had to cut. Saudi Arabia, the largest producer, became the swing producer. Its output fell from 9.9 million barrels a day in 1980 to 3.4 million in 1985: down by two-thirds. The rest of OPEC cut far less, and producers outside OPEC grew. The price drifted down anyway, and Saudi Arabia's oil income, at those prices, fell to about a quarter. At the end of 1985 it stopped cutting and opened the taps. Within months, a barrel fell from about 31 dollars to 12. Holding the price up had cost Saudi Arabia its market share; letting it go cost everyone, including itself, but stopped the bleeding of share. That is the cartel's problem: each member gains by producing more while the others hold back.

The same dilemma returned. When shale oil flooded the market after 2014, Saudi Arabia did not cut. It produced more, and the price halved. In 2016 OPEC began coordinating with other producers, Russia the largest, a group known as OPEC plus. In April 2020, with the world locked down, OPEC plus agreed the biggest cut in its history, 9.7 million barrels a day, and OPEC's own output fell by six million barrels a day in a single month. And in 2026 it was not a decision but a war that took OPEC's oil off the market. A cartel can choose to hold back. It cannot choose what happens to the strait.
Shale: Chapter eleven. Shale: oil from a factory.

In 2008 the United States produced about five million barrels of crude a day, half its peak of 1970, and everyone expected the decline to go on. Then drillers in Texas and North Dakota combined two old techniques, drilling sideways and cracking the rock with water and sand under pressure, and turned them on the source rock itself. Between 2008 and 2025, North Dakota's output rose about 7-fold and Texas's about 5-fold. In 2018 American production passed its 1970 peak, and by 2026 it was close to fourteen million barrels a day. No country has ever produced more crude oil, as the Energy Information Administration has noted every year since 2018.

The price collapse of 2014 was the test. Drillers cut fast. The number of rigs drilling for oil in America fell by 80 percent in nineteen months. Output fell by only about a tenth, and not for long. The wells drilled were better, the rigs that stayed were the best, and the companies drilled their best rock first. By 2018, output was setting records with half the rigs of 2014. Shale is a factory process: thousands of nearly identical wells, each a few months from decision to oil, getting cheaper and more productive each year.

And it changed the country's place in the world. In 2005, America imported, net, 12.5 million barrels a day of crude and fuels. Since 2020 it has exported more than it imports. And shale changed the price, too. A deepwater project decided today produces in the 2030s. A shale well decided today produces next spring. When prices rise, American drillers can add supply within months, which puts a soft ceiling on the price; when they fall, they stop just as fast. The swing producer of the 1980s was a government. Today a large part of the swing is thousands of private drillers, each looking at the price.
Refining: Chapter twelve. Refining: a business of spreads.

Crude oil is no use as it comes out of the ground. A refinery turns it into things people buy. The first step is a tall column. Crude is heated until most of it boils, and the vapour rises up the tower, cooling as it goes. Heavy molecules condense low down: fuel oil and asphalt at the bottom, then diesel, then jet fuel, then gasoline, and the lightest gases at the top. Then other units break the heavy cuts into lighter, more valuable ones. The result is that a refinery's whole business is a spread: what its products sell for, minus what the crude cost.

Traders measure that spread with a rule of thumb, the three-two-one crack: three barrels of crude make roughly two of gasoline and one of diesel. Here it is, month by month since 1987, from New York Harbor's fuel prices and Brent. Through the 1990s it was usually under ten dollars a barrel. In 2020, with nobody driving or flying, the spread fell to 8 dollars a barrel on average; in 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine cut supplies of diesel, it averaged 35. In 2026, with the Gulf's exports of diesel and jet fuel cut off, it has averaged 39 so far. A refiner's profit follows the spread, not the price of oil. Valero, one of America's largest refiners, lost money in 2020 and made eleven and a half billion dollars in 2022. Pipelines are the opposite: in America the rates on oil pipelines between states are regulated, so they earn a toll on every barrel, whatever it is worth.
Gas: Chapter thirteen. Gas, and the ships that made it global.

Natural gas comes out of the same rocks as oil, often from the same wells. But for most of its history it has had not one price but several. In Louisiana, at the pipeline hub called Henry Hub, gas has mostly cost a few dollars per million British thermal units. In Europe and in Asia it usually cost two or three times as much. And in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine and most of its pipeline gas to Europe stopped, Europe's price rose to 70 dollars, while in Louisiana it was 9. The same molecules, eight times the price. Why didn't traders just ship the cheap gas to the dear market?

Because gas is hard to move. Oil is a liquid you can pour into any tanker. Gas fills pipes, and pipes stop at the coast. To cross an ocean it has to be cooled to about minus a hundred and sixty-two degrees, when it becomes a liquid, about six hundred times smaller. That takes a plant costing billions of dollars. Then special ships with insulated tanks, and at the other end a terminal to warm it back into gas. Each step costs money, so the gap between the cheap market and the dear one has to be wide enough to pay for the chain. Until enough plants and ships exist, the gap can stay open for years.

America built that chain. Its first big export plant, on the Louisiana coast, shipped its first cargoes in 2016. By 2025 the country was exporting about 15 billion cubic feet of liquefied gas a day; since 2023 it has been the world's largest exporter. Cheniere, the company that built that first plant, saw its revenue nearly double in 2022, to 33 billion dollars, as Europe bid for every cargo. Shale gas from Texas and Pennsylvania now sets a floor under prices in Europe and Asia: the price of gas at Henry Hub, plus the cost of the chain. Gas is becoming, slowly, one market, the way oil already is.
Services: Oil companies decide where to drill. Mostly, other companies do the drilling. They rent out rigs and crews, pump the water and sand that crack the shale, measure the rock as the bit goes down, cement the wells, and build the equipment for the sea floor. The biggest are SLB, which used to be called Schlumberger, Halliburton, and Baker Hughes. Their customers' spending is their revenue, and their customers' spending is the first thing to be cut when the price falls.

Here is the 2014 bust from their side. The number of oil rigs working in America fell by almost three-quarters in two years. Halliburton's revenue fell by 52 percent, and SLB's by 43. In 2016 Halliburton lost 5.8 billion dollars. And in 2020 it happened again. Compare ExxonMobil's own capital spending, in grey: it fell too, but its business kept producing and selling oil from the wells it already had. A service company's business is the new wells. Part 6's accelerator works here as it does for the makers of machines: a fall in spending on new capacity hits hardest the companies that sell it.
Landscape: Here is the industry as of November 2026. The national oil companies, owned by states, led by Saudi Aramco, which earned more in 2025 than the 11 companies on this page that file their accounts in America, put together. The majors: ExxonMobil and Chevron in America, Shell, BP and TotalEnergies in Europe, each producing, refining and selling around the world. The independents, many of them shale drillers in Texas and New Mexico. The refiners, living on the crack spread. The service companies, living on everyone else's capital spending. The liquefied gas exporters. And the traders, private companies most people have never heard of, who buy, store and ship oil and fuel between all the others.

And the market itself, in November 2026. At the worst of the war, in May, almost eleven million barrels a day were shut in across the Middle East; by October, two and a half. Brent averaged a hundred and twenty-four dollars in October, and fell back below a hundred in early November. Oil has found other ways out of the Gulf: across Saudi Arabia by pipeline, and from ship to ship along the coast of Oman. The world used about two million barrels a day less oil this year than last. The Energy Information Administration expects Brent to average about 86 dollars in 2027, as flows recover and stocks are rebuilt. That forecast is the one this part will make a call against.
Called: Perhaps the most famous oil forecast of all was made in March 1956, in a hotel in San Antonio, by a Shell geologist, M. King Hubbert. He had the record of American production to 1956. He argued that a field's, or a country's, output rises and falls in a bell shape, and that the area under the bell is the oil that will ever come out. If America held a hundred and fifty billion barrels in all, its output would peak around 1965. Even if it held two hundred billion, the peak would come only around 1970. Then American production peaked in 1970, at 9.64 million barrels a day, almost exactly on his upper curve, and fell for nearly forty years. And then shale. By 2025 production was 13.7 million barrels a day, and the United States had produced 258 billion barrels, more than either of Hubbert's totals. He was right about the date of the peak and wrong about the end, because he could not count oil that the technology of 1956 could not produce.

He made a world forecast too. With twelve hundred and fifty billion barrels in all, world output would peak at about the year 2000. It did not. In 2025 the world produced 84.5 million barrels of crude a day, more than ever. Higher prices kept paying for new ways to reach oil that had once been out of reach: deep water, oil sands, shale. The lesson is not that peaks never come. It is that the ceiling of a resource is set by price and technology as much as by geology.

And this series' own call. Brent crude will average less than ninety dollars a barrel in 2027. The Energy Information Administration expects about 86. For it: the oil shut in has fallen from almost eleven million barrels a day to two and a half, demand is recovering, and stocks are being rebuilt. Against it: the strait is still at risk, stocks start the year low, and this chapter has shown how hard a small shortage can move the price. We put it at 60 percent, and will score it in January 2028.
